title: Magmatic underplating and crustal intrusions accommodate extension during Red Sea continental rifting

paper_content.abstract: Magmatism’s role in continental rupture and ocean formation remains a critical question in Earth Sciences. The Red Sea, where Arabia is rifting from Nubia, offers an ideal setting to explore this process. This study analyses geochemical and isotopic data from gabbros and basaltic dikes in the Tihama Asir complex, formed during early Red Sea rifting (Late Oligocene). The results show that asthenospheric melts assimilated ancient lower crust before rising into shallow magma chambers with minimal upper crustal contamination. Rising asthenosphere driven by the Afar plume and by extensional stresses thermally weakened the lower crust, allowing it to decouple from the mantle, causing depth-dependent deformation. The generated asthenospheric melts underplated and intruded the thinning continental crust protracting continental rifting by re-thickening of the crust and accommodating extension. This study provides the evidence of tholeiitic underplating beneath thick continental crust during early rifting, substantially postponing the onset of seafloor spreading.
paper_content.introduction:
Over billions of years, the Earth’s internal processes cyclically formed and broke apart supercontinents, leading to the birth of new oceans. The Wilson Cycle explains how continents split, forming passive margins1,2. Continental fragmentation takes place due to extensional stress, initiating rifts where the lithosphere is affected by progressive mechanical deformation and magmatic processes. This process continues until the continental lithosphere ultimately fractures, creating new oceanic lithosphere that separates two conjugate juvenile continental margins. The East African Rift System, including the Red Sea, represents various stages of this process, from continental rifts to an emerging ocean. This rift system began fragmenting the Afro-Arabian shield since the late Oligocene, influenced by a mantle plume impacting the Afar region around 34 Ma3–5. Magnetic anomalies in the Red Sea suggest an ongoing formation of oceanic crust, with the southern region reaching further in this process than the central or northern regions6–8. Variations in the amount of extension may reflect different stages of the rifting process, while differences in GNSS-derived relative velocities between the Arabian and Nubian plates, increasing from ~7 mm/yr in the northern Red Sea to ~16 mm/yr in the southern Red Sea9 suggest distinct dominant mechanisms for the formation of the northern and southern Red Sea. The onset of rifting in the Red Sea was preceded by flood basalts erupted in Ethiopia, NE Sudan, and SW Yemen5, also associated with rhyolitic volcanism10,11. Abundant melt was injected into the Arabian basement in the early stages of rifting (26–21 Ma)5,12–15 as testified by the occurrence of thousands of kilometers-long dike swarms running NW-SE parallel to the Arabian coast of the Red Sea12,16, along with the contemporaneous Tihama Asir12 (southern Red Sea), Al Lith16 (central Red Sea), and Quseir13,14 (northern Red Sea) magmatic complexes, which include gabbros, basaltic dikes, and granophyres. Widespread gabbro and dike injection was followed by successive phases of volcanism, leading to the formation of extensive alkali-basalt lava fields (harrats). Some of these phases had finite eruption periods, while others began at different times and continued into recent history12,16–20 (Fig. 1).

The formation of a magma-rich margin during rifting is driven by multiple geological factors21,22. A key factor is the magmatic supply, where sufficient magma generation from the mantle is essential for processes like dike injection and underplating (i.e., addition of mafic magma to the lower crust and uppermost mantle around the Moho in the form of batholiths and sill-like structures23). Efficient heat transfer from the mantle can promote localized melting and assimilation of crustal material, affecting the formation of transitional crust. The composition and thickness of the pre-existing continental crust affect how it interacts with ascending magmas, while the rheological properties of the lithosphere, such as its strength and viscosity, impact deformation behavior. The duration of rifting, the divergence rate and magmatic activity also play a critical role24. Understanding these constraints is fundamental for modeling magma-rich margin formation and predicting their evolution.

The Tihama Asir magmatic complex in southernmost Saudi Arabia serves as a key location to study the initial phase of syn-rift magmatism and its influence on the geodynamic evolution of the southern Red Sea rift system (Fig. 1), and, more broadly, of magma-rich rift systems. This region provides insights into the interplay between magmatic supply, tectonic setting, heat transfer, and crustal composition during the early stages of rifting12. In this study, we present geochemical data including bulk rock major and trace elements, as well as Sr, Nd, and Pb isotopic compositions of the Tihama Asir gabbros and dykes, in order to investigate the magma source and its migration and emplacement within the crust during rifting. We also measured the magnetic properties of these rocks to better constrain the geophysical signals they produce. Additionally, 40Ar/39Ar age determinations, combined with existing geophysical data, enable us to reconstruct the evolution of the magmatic complex within the broader framework of Red Sea rifting and ocean basin development.
paper_content.results:
The Tihama Asir igneous complex
The Tihama Asir magmatic complex is located east of the Jizan coastal plain in southwestern Saudi Arabia (Fig. 1). It consists of various layered gabbroic bodies with compositional layering ranging from relatively primitive olivine gabbros to more evolved lithologies such as oxide gabbros, with layering occurring at meter- to decameter-scale and tending to diminish up-section, akin to typical Penrose-type ophiolite stratigraphy25–27. The gabbros are in primary contact with granophyre granitic intrusions, with preserved intrusive contacts to the strongly faulted Arabian Shield Neoproterozoic basement comprising Pan-African granitoids, low-grade metamorphic rocks, and gneisses26. Diffuse basaltic to rhyolitic dike swarms locally overlay the gabbroic lithologies and intrude the continental basement12,26,27. Our 40Ar/39Ar age determination of 26.03±0.54 Ma and recalibrated previous 40Ar/39Ar datings28 of the Tihama Asir intrusive rocks and the dike swarms constrain their age to within the range 26–21 Ma (Supplementary Fig. S1; Supplementary Data S1). Faulting in this area is suggested to have begun around 29 Ma15, just a few million years prior to the formation of the magmatic complex. This temporal relationship implies that the Tihama Asir magmatic complex formed due to extensive magmatism during the early stages of Red Sea continental rifting12,27–29.

Petrology and geochemistry
The most primitive Tihama Asir olivine gabbros show petrological and geochemical characteristics consistent with formation from tholeiitic parental melts, resembling modern MORBs (Supplementary Data S2). However, the evolved gabbros and oxide gabbros show saturation of phlogopite and selective enrichments in LREE and highly incompatible elements (Rb, Ba, U, Th, Nb, Sr, K). The geochemical evolution of the parental melts diverged progressively from that of oceanic tholeiites, suggesting a gradual assimilation of continental crust during the emplacement of the gabbroic bodies (Fig. 2). Similarly, the dike swarms overlying the gabbros (sheeted dike complex) exhibit transitional affinity, with selective enrichments in LREE and highly incompatible elements compared to Red Sea MORB and sub-chondritic Nb-Ta/LREE ratios. These dikes are in chemical equilibrium with the clinopyroxene in the gabbros and are interpreted as melts extracted from hybridized gabbroic crystal mush after high degrees of contamination from upper crustal material.

Furthermore, meter-scale anastomosed basaltic dikes crosscut the gabbros with irregular chilled boundaries, locally dissecting and embaying portions of the host rock (e.g., TA-02/Dy-1; see Fig. 2c). These basalts display a chemical composition indicative of limited fractionation in magma chambers and nearly flat PM-normalized incompatible trace element patterns, akin to present-day enriched MORBs31 (Fig. 2). Being close to chemical equilibrium with the clinopyroxene from the most primitive gabbros, these basalts are considered poorly fractionated mantle melts that escaped crustal contamination and were injected into the cooling gabbroic crystal mush soon after its emplacement30.

Radiogenic isotopes
The Tihama Asir gabbros exhibit higher initial (i.e., present-day values recalculated to their crystallization age; Supplementary Data S3) 87Sr/86Sr (0.7033–0.7037) and lower initial 143Nd/144Nd (0.51292–0.51296) ratios compared to those of Red Sea MORB32–34 and the Cenozoic alkaline magmatism in the northern Arabian plate19,20,35–40. Nonetheless, their initial 206Pb/204Pb and 207Pb/204Pb ratios plot amongst the most depleted samples from the Red Sea MORB and the Cenozoic volcanism from northern Arabia (Fig. 3). The gabbros isotopically resemble the inferred compositions of the Afar plume41–43 in terms of Nd and Sr isotopes, albeit they are less radiogenic in Pb. These compositions (Supplementary Data S3) suggest a source with relatively high time-integrated Rb/Sr and low Sm/Nd ratios compared to those of the northern Red Sea basalts, but with similarly low U–Th/Pb ratios. Interestingly, a basaltic dike (TA-02/Dy-1) cutting across the gabbros exhibits Sr–Nd–Pb isotopes nearly coincident with those of the inferred Afar plume (Fig. 3), supporting the idea that primary melts of the Tihama Asir formed from an asthenospheric source near the main impingement area of the Afar plume30. Upon closer examination, selected gabbroic samples gradually diverge from the crosscutting dike along trends of decreasing Sr–Nd and Pb isotope ratios. These isotopic signatures suggest contamination by material with ancient depletions in Rb/Sr and U/Th/Pb, coupled with relatively low Sm/Nd ratios, compositions commonly attributed to lower continental crustal material, such as the ancient lower continental crustal granulite xenoliths locally sampled within the Cenozoic volcanism of the Arabian plate25.

In contrast, samples from the sheeted dike complex have much higher initial 87Sr/86Sr (0.7038–0.7047) and lower initial 143Nd/144Nd (0.51284–0.51293) ratios compared to those of gabbros, yet they exhibit similar Pb isotope ratios. These samples cluster within the Nd–Sr and Pb isotopic space of the widespread volcanism in South Arabia and Yemen, well-known examples of Afar-type magma strongly contaminated by both upper and lower continental crust41,42. Given that these rocks display intrusive contacts with upper crustal lithologies and show selective enrichments in highly incompatible elements and LREE compared to the gabbros, we infer that their melts were generated within melt-rich zones of the gabbroic crystal mush and might have further assimilated Pan-African upper continental crust. Indeed, their Sr–Nd-Pb compositions fall between those of the Tihama Asir intrusives and the Pan-African granitoids (Fig. 3). Our hypothesis is corroborated by combined radiogenic Nd–Sr–Pb and δ18O isotopes of flood volcanics from Yemen42, which exhibit the same extent of isotopic variations observed in the Tihama Asir gabbros (Fig. 3). The less contaminated Yemenite basalts retain mantle-like δ18O isotopes and Sr–Nd and Pb isotopic ratios indicative of an Afar-like upper mantle. In contrast, those retaining evidence of crustal contamination have high δ18O isotopes42 and diverge along two different trends, aligned towards enriched and depleted Pb compositions, indicating contamination by upper and lower Pan-African crust, respectively.

Assimilation-fractional crystallization model
We conducted assimilation-fractional crystallization (AFC) modeling following the approach outlined by ref. 44. Specifically tailored to simulate the chemical evolution of a magmatic system undergoing fractional crystallization alongside assimilation of wall rocks (Figs. 4 and 5). We utilized the average compositions of lower crustal granulite xenoliths42 and Pan-African granitoids45 as the assimilated components, and the crosscutting basaltic dike displaying Afar-like compositions as the initial melt (for further details, see Methods). The isotopic trends observed in the Tihama Asir gabbros are faithfully reproduced across all different Nd–Sr–Pb isotopic spaces at low degrees of assimilation of lower crustal granulites, considering mass assimilated/mass crystallized ratios ranging from 0.7 to 0.9 (Fig. 4), and utilizing the same geochemical parameters used to replicate the trace element enrichments30.

Conversely, the high Sr and low Nd isotopes observed in the sheeted dikes necessitate additional assimilation of Pan-African granitoids, commencing from the hybrid melts that formed the gabbros. Notably, our model adeptly reproduces the distinct trends of the gabbros and dike swarms concerning Nd and Sr versus ΔPb (7/4) (Fig. 4b). The low 206Pb/204Pb ratios and comparatively high 207Pb/204Pb ratios of lower crustal granulites in the Arabian plate42 result in a gradual increase in ΔPb (7/4) as 143Nd/144Nd ratios decrease. Conversely, the upper crustal Pan-African granitoids have 206Pb/204Pb and 207Pb/204Pb lying on the NHRL45, thus producing a local decrease in ΔPb (7/4).
paper_content.methods:
40Ar/39Ar dating
Age determinations were performed at the Laboratoire des Sciences du Climat et de l’Environnement facility (CNRS-CEA, Gif-sur-Yvette), France.

Sample preparation
40Ar/39Ar measurements were performed on the microcrystalline groundmass of the sample, considered representative of the phase that crystallized during lava solidification. Samples were crushed, sieved (250–125 mm size), and washed in 1N acetic acid at 60 °C for 40 minutes to remove secondary mineral phases. Phenocrysts and xenocrysts, carrying an excess of 40Ar, were removed using heavy liquids (Diiodomethane) and magnetic separations. Absence of alteration phases was verified using a binocular microscope.

Procedure
Splits of 120–130 mg were wrapped in 99.5% copper foil, loaded in aluminum disks, and irradiated in the CLICIT facility at Oregon State University’s TRIGA reactor for 10 h. After irradiation, samples were degassed at 550-650 °C to remove atmospheric argon. Neutron fluence (J) was monitored using FCs crystals, with J values calculated from 6 single crystal laser fusion analyses, reported in Supplementary Data S1. Age calculations used the decay constants from ref. 75 and an atmospheric 40Ar/36Ar ratio of 298.56 from ref. 76. Precision of mass discrimination correction was monitored by daily air argon measurements, achieving about 0.1–0.15% (1σ standard deviation).

Pure groundmass aliquots were incrementally heated in 10 steps between 650 °C and 1200 °C using a metal resistance furnace. Isotopic measurements were performed using a high-sensitivity GV5400 instrument in ion counting mode. An analytical run consisted of 20 peak scans of each argon isotope with integration times 2 s (40Ar, 39Ar), 10 s (37Ar, 38Ar, baseline) and 20 s (36Ar). This was preceded by a peak centering routine on the five Ar isotopes upon sample admission into the mass spectrometer. Raw argon isotope abundances were regressed back to inlet time using NG software (v. 2.90). System blanks measured prior to step-heating ranged from 6.8×10−16 to 1.2×10−15 moles of 40Ar and 2.5·10-18 to 6.2×10−18 moles of 36Ar, which were substantially lower than sample signals.

Results
Plateau ages, isochron regressions, probability of fit estimates and errors were calculated using ArArCalc77 following the criteria defined in ref. 78. Results of the step heating experiment are detailed in the Supplementary Data S1. The plateau age for sample TA-06/Dy-1, calculated from 66.4% of gas released, excluded the first three and last steps due to anomalously young apparent ages likely caused by 40Ar* loss from subtle alteration. The preferred age for this sample is the plateau age of 26.03±0.54 Ma (2σ uncertainty).

Re-evaluation of Ar–Ar literature dates using updated standards
40Ar/39Ar ages from ref. 28. were originally calibrated against an age of 17.25±0.20 Ma for the Bern 4B biotite standard, which corresponds to an age of 126.6±4.2 Ma for LP-679. Initially, Bern 4B’s age was recalibrated using the ArAR software80, considering an updated age of 127.5 Ma for LP-6, which equates to an age of 28.10±0.04 Ma for FCTs. This recalibration increased the age of Bern 4B to 17.38±0.20 Ma. This age was further recalculated using the FCTs age applied in this study (28.201±0.023 Ma81). Based on this calculation, the age of Bern 4B is adjusted to 17.44±0.20 Ma. This updated age was used to recalculate the ages reported by ref. 28. using the ArAR software. For consistency, we also applied the constant values from ref. 75. in the calculation (Supplementary Data S1).

Bulk rock major, trace elements, and Sr, Nd, and Pb isotope compositions
The bulk rock major and trace element compositions of the Tihama Asir gabbros and sheeted dikes are sourced from ref. 30. and were analyzed using XRF and ICP-mass spectrometry at Activation Laboratories Ltd., Ancaster, Ontario (Supplementary Data S2), following the analytical techniques detailed on the company’s website (www.actlabs.com).

Bulk rock Sr, Nd, and Pb isotope analyses were conducted at the Dipartimento di Scienze della Terra, University of Florence. Sample powders (approximately 250 mg each) were taken from the same aliquots used for major and trace element determinations. The samples were leached with 1M HCl in an ultrasonic bath and rinsed several times with MilliQ water to minimize potential contributions from secondary phases that could have altered the magma signature. The samples were dissolved through sequential HF–HNO3–HCl dissolution, and the Sr, Nd, and Pb fractions were purified through standard liquid chromatographic techniques.

Isotopic ratios were determined using thermal ionization mass spectrometry (Thermo-Fisher Scientific Triton Plus). Mass fractionation of Sr and Nd isotopes was exponentially corrected with 86Sr/88Sr=0.1194 and 146Nd/144Nd=0.7219, respectively. Interferences of 87Rb and 144Sm on 87Sr and 144Nd, respectively, were monitored by measuring 85Rb and 147Sm. Due to their extremely low abundances (when present) these masses were measured on 1013 Ohm amplifiers; such interferences resulted negligible for all the samples. All other masses were measured on 1011 Ohm amplifiers. The within-run 87Sr/86Sr average value for NBS 987 reference material was 0.710255±7 (2σ, n=4), and the 143Nd/144Nd average value for the internal standard NdFi was 0.511465±3 (2σ, n=3). Accuracy and precision were further checked by measuring the isotope ratios of international rock standards BHVO-1 (87Sr/86Sr=0.703484±6; 143Nd/144Nd=0.512986±9) and BCR-2 (87Sr/86Sr=0.705018±7; 143Nd/144Nd=0.512620±5).

Lead isotopic composition was measured by collecting the smaller 204Pb beam on 1013 Ohm amplifier and the other masses (206Pb, 207Pb, and 208Pb) on 1011 Ohm amplifiers. Instrumental mass bias was corrected using replicate analyses of NIST SRM 981 standard, yielding an average fractionation factor of 0.135% (±0.010%) per mass unit relative to the reference values, which was applied to all Pb isotopic ratios. The accuracy of the Pb isotope measurements was tested through replicate analyses of international reference material BHVO-1 (206Pb/204Pb=18.705±4, 207Pb/204Pb=15.577±5, 208Pb/204Pb=38.375±15). All the isotope ratios of the reference materials are reported in Supplementary Data S3 and are identical within error to previously published values82,83.

All the isotope ratios were recalculated to their initial values, assumed to correspond to the time of the rock formation. The formation ages of the studied samples were estimated based on the available Ar–Ar ages of the associated lithological units (this work and recalibrated ages of ref. 28. (Supplementary Data S1). For the age correction, we specifically re-measured the elemental Rb/Sr, Sm/Nd, U/Pb, and Th/Pb ratios on the leached samples using ICP-MS (7800 Agilent) at the University of Florence. A small aliquot of the same sample solution used for isotopic measurements was collected (after complete dissolution and before chemical separation), evaporated, and diluted in 2% HNO3 for ICP-MS analyses. Replicate analyses of international reference materials BHVO-1 and AGV-1 yielded Rb/Sr, U/Pb, Th/Pb, and Sm/Nd ratios consistent with reference values of ref. 84. and with reproducibility <4% (2σ). The internal errors (2σ) of the age-corrected Sr, Nd, and Pb isotope ratios for all samples were fully propagated to account for uncertainties in age, isotopic ratios, and elemental contents. Total procedure blanks for Sr, Nd, and Pb were 60 pg, 12 pg, and 43 pg, respectively. The data and associated uncertainties are reported in Supplementary Data S3.

Assimilation-fractional crystallization model
The enrichments in highly incompatible elements (e.g., Rb, Ba, Th, U, Zr, Hf) and the positive LREE/HREE fractionation observed in the melts in equilibrium with the Tihama Asir clinopyroxenes can be effectively reproduced by a process involving the assimilation of lower and upper continental crust, combined with fractional crystallization of a gabbroic assemblage (i.e., olivine, plagioclase, and clinopyroxene)30. A similar geochemical model is applied here to assess whether the assimilation of lower and upper continental crust can explain the isotopic compositions of the Tihama Asir gabbros and the associated sheeted dike.

The trace element (Sm, Nd, Rb, Sr, Th, U, and Pb) and initial Nd–Sr–Pb isotopic compositions of the melts generated during the two scenarios above (assimilation of lower and/or upper crust) were calculated using an assimilation-fractional crystallization (AFC) process, following the equations of ref. 44. For the assimilation of the lower crust, we used the basalts (TA-02/Dy-1) crosscutting the Tihama Asir gabbros at a high angle as the starting melt composition. These basalts, unmodified by any crustal contamination process, exhibit an EMORB-like trace element pattern and isotopic composition similar to that of the inferred Afar plume43. Conversely, the starting melt composition for the assimilation of upper crust has a Nd–Sr–Pb isotopic composition coinciding with the average isotopic composition of the Tihama Asir gabbros and is similar to melts extracted from the gabbros after 5–10% degrees of lower crustal contamination. The composition of the melt modified by the AFC process was calculated at 1% increments, representing the remaining melt mass (scaled from 100% to 0), corresponding to ‘F’ in the equation from ref. 44. Each of the two AFC scenarios was calculated using the mean and extreme (±1σ) compositions of the lower and upper crust assimilants42,45. The AFC scenarios were modeled with different Ma/Mc ratios of 0.9, 0.8, and 0.7, shown in Fig. 4 in red, blue, and gray, respectively. Parameters and results are provided in Supplementary Data S4.

Magnetic properties
Magnetic properties, including natural remanent magnetization (NRM) and volume-specific magnetic susceptibility (K), were measured on 14 rock samples at the paleomagnetic lab of ISMAR-CNR in Bologna, Italy. Four samples (marked AR) of basaltic dikes were hand-oriented in the field using a magnetic compass. In the laboratory, between 1 and 5 standard paleomagnetic cylinders (2.54×2.2 cm) were drilled from each rock sample, resulting in a total of 31 specimens. The NRM was measured with a PSM spinner magnetometer, while magnetic susceptibility (K) was determined using a Bartington MS2B meter. The Koenigsberger ratio (Q) was calculated as the ratio of remanent magnetization (NRM) to the induced magnetization produced by Earth’s field (26.506 A/m). Results are presented in Supplementary Fig. S3 and Supplementary Data S5.

Data availability
All the data generated in this study are provided in the Supplementary Data files (from S1 to S5) and have also been deposited in Figshare https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.29410169.

Code availability
The Assimilation-fractional crystallization (AFC) model code (alpha-MELTS), which can be used to re-produce the data presented here (Supplementary Data S4), is available on GitHub https://github.com/magmasource/alphaMELTS.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
I had the pleasure of reading "Parting continents: lower-crustal intrusions delayed continental rupture in the Red Sea" by
Alessio Sanfilippo and others, and I thank both the editor and authors for the opportunity to contemplate on this manuscript
and provide some feedback. In this manuscript, the authors present new argon dates, magnetic data, geochemical data
including bulk rock elemental, Sr, Nd, and Pb isotopic data, and modelling of these data to investigate the evolution of the
Tihama Asir igneous complex in Saudi Arabia within the broader context of Red Sea formation and ocean basin
development. These new data, and in particular the isotopic (Sr-Nd-Pb-Ar) data provide a valuable contribution to efforts in
understanding the vast and complex petrogenesis of igneous complexes in Saudi Arabia and, as such, are of high value to
this journal. The authors take a unique and effective approach in this task by interpreting their varied data sources together
with published literature data, thus presenting a dynamic and multi-dimensional interpretation that is compelling and
supported by their data. The methods are detailed and are highly appropriate to this work. The authors outline an evolution
of the Red Sea spanning the Oligocene-Miocene wherein the variable spreading rates of the Southern and Northern Red
Sea are explained by weakening of the lithosphere in the south due to impingement of the Afar Plume and collision in the
north of the plate. Thermal weakening of lithosphere combined with asthenospheric upwelling initiated magmatism that
accommodated extension and ultimately delayed oceanic crust formation by several million years. These results have a high
degree of significance for our understanding of ocean basin formation and are thus fitting for this journal.
I would, however, make several suggestions for re-framing certain aspects of this manuscript before acceptance by the
journal. Overall the manuscript is very well written and individual thoughts are easy to understand. I had the greatest degree
of confusion with the organization of the manuscript. While it flows logically, the lack of clearly defined sections makes it
difficult to know when the authors are specifically referencing their own data and when they are still talking about published
data. For instance, the first paragraph on page 6 blends a discussion on both existing data in the literature and also the
authors new data, which is not at all clear. Upon first read it sounds like the authors are still discussing published data but
without necessary references to support their observations, but then later on it becomes apparent that they are discussing
their new data. The confusion is driven by two issues: 1) the lack of a clearly-defined results and discussion section, and 2)
abundant mixing of introduction-type rhetoric with new observations (results-type rhetoric) and interpretations (discussion-
type rhetoric) by the authors. Again using this section as an example, on page 5 the authors walk through an introduction on
the Tihama Asir igneous complex but then later within the same section present new observations and interpretations which
make it difficult to clearly understand when something they are saying is novel or an accepted interpretation gleaned from
literature. The manuscript would thus benefit from a general re-organization to make it easier on the reader to follow the
authors' thoughts. For instance, a clear conclusion section would be greatly appreciated.
Another general criticism is the lack of a substantial discussion on the application of the authors' model on a global scale.
The authors briefly mention the names of other regions that may have experienced a similar geologic history in the very last
paragraph of the manuscript, but they do not discuss any details on why they consider these regions to be worth mentioning. A
small subsection within the discussion that highlights the broader implications of the findings in this paper, other regions in
the world that are or have experienced a similar geologic history, and details on how this model can be applied to those
regions, would greatly enhance this manuscript and increase its suitability for this (or any) journal.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
DISCLAIMER
I am not an igneous petrologist/geochemist/isotope specialist. As agreed with the editor, I therefore focused on the regional
aspect and the discussion about rifting processes but didn’t look in detail at the methods and results. However, I did
comment when a link between results and interpretation was not clear to me. As this journal has a broad audience (I also
think you are submitting your paper here to reach more than igneous petrologists), these comments might flag some parts of
the argumentation that might not be properly phrased or explained for non-experts.
Note that I made a number of suggestions to increase clarity or completeness of the manuscript. Use them if you find them
useful, but forget them if you don’t agree with them.
REVIEW SUMMARY
Sanfilippo et al. present a manuscript on a Cenozoic magmatic complex on the passive margin of the Red Sea. This
structure is one of the few rift-related igneous complexes cropping out and available to study magma-rich rifting processes
and the rift-to-drift transition. They apply petrological, geochemical and isotopic methods to investigate the emplacement of
this igneous complex, including melt pathways and crustal contamination. They derive a model for the formation of the Red
Sea passive margin, where the magmatic intrusions increase the thickness of the crust, forming a proto-oceanic crust. They
finally propose that these magmatic intrusions delay seafloor spreading.
Overall, the object of the study is rare, interesting, and its analysis is novel. The topic will appeal to a broad range of
geologists working on rift and passive margins and won’t be limited to igneous petrologists only.
I am not qualified to judge the methodology. The links between the results and some of the interpretations are not clear to
me. This does not necessarily mean that these interpretations are wrong, but maybe that this link is not explicitly phrased for
non-experts. I’ll leave the other reviewer(s) judge the validity of these aspects, but I encourage the authors to rephrase these
argumentations for the broader audience.
The final interpretation of the authors is that this magmatic activity significantly delayed oceanic spreading. I question this
interpretation as the delayed nature of oceanic spreading in the southern Red Sea is far from clear and several arguments
indicate a rather quick transition to oceanic spreading compared to other margins worldwide and other parts of the Red Sea.
The link between magmatism and delay is also not clear. I would advise the authors to either leave out this part of the
interpretation and focus on other interesting aspects, such as magma-assisted extension, or to present a robust
argumentation.
Finally, it is regrettable that the authors completely omit one of the prominent hypotheses for the extent and the age of
oceanic spreading in the Red Sea and I think this should be corrected.
More detailed comments are listed below.
GENERAL COMMENTS
General message of the paper
This is certainly not the most important point of this review, but I think that one aspect that could be improved is to better
explain to the reader what your main message is. Nature Communication has a very broad audience, and you should make
clear to them what your message is and why it does matter. You should be very explicit as to why your work is novel, and
what it brings to the understanding of rifting processes. Sentences like “We show that...”, or “Our results confirm [for the first
time] that...” or “Our results indicate that previous hypotheses were probably incorrect because...”.
The main message of the paper was not clear to me after the first read.
This is particularly visible in the paragraph starting with “Although several questions remain, our work allows to outline the
evolution of the southern Red Sea rift…” where you present the whole evolution of the margin but where it is not clear what
your contribution is to the story (detailed comment below).
You might also want to improve the end of your introduction. You correctly report the numerous factors that play a role in the
rift to drift transition (that part might even be slightly shortened if you must save some characters for the total count), but you
don’t say specifically how this study site and your analyses are crucial for this understanding. I think it would better “sell”
your study and help the reader understand to purpose and value of your study if you put more emphasis on the uniqueness
of your study area and the novelty of your analyses, e.g. what you present later in your manuscript “most constraints on the
location and depth of magma intrusions during the initial stages of rifting have been derived from crustal-scale seismic
imaging of relatively young (e.g., Ethiopian) and poorly evolved (e.g., Baikal) rifts.”. Then (still in the intro), I'd explain in more
detail what you did. Something like “We conduct XYZ analyses to unravel XYZ, the source of the magma and its migration
and emplacement in the crust. Then we measured XYZ to better constrain the geophysical signal these rocks can produce”.
So that afterwards, the reader knows more precisely what exactly you investigated.
Just a suggestion to make it more attractive.
Link between results and interpretations
I sometimes miss the link between your results and some of your interpretations. It might just be because I am not an expert
in igneous geochemistry/isotopes, but the audience of the journal is also very broad and other readers might also have
difficulties following your reasoning.
I have done detailed comments on these cases below under “Specific comments”. Some are important points for your
interpretation and should thus be addressed: E.g.: How do your results allow you to interpret that the lithospheric mantle was
already completely replaced by asthenospheric mantle? Which results allow you to say that the ascent of the magma
through the crust was fast?
Without clarification and as a non-expert in these methods, I fail to completely understand how your results support some
of your interpretations.
Age of oceanic spreading in the Red Sea
One important paragraph of the paper deals with the age of oceanic spreading in the Red Sea. You conclude that oceanic
spreading started around 5 Ma. The problem is that you omit one of the main hypotheses about the structure of the
(southern) Red Sea. In the paper, you present two hypotheses, the 5 Ma oceanic crust hypothesis and the “two-stage”
oceanic crust hypothesis. I agree with you that the latter is not plausible from a timing and kinematic point of view (you could
even shorten this argumentation if you’d need more space). But you completely omit the hypothesis of an onset of oceanic
spreading between 10 and 14 Ma. This hypothesis has seen a lot of attention since the 80s and in the last decade. Many
serious publications argue for such an interpretation
They estimate the initiation of seafloor spreading around 10 Ma (Okwokwo et al., 2022), between 10-12 Ma (Izzeldin,
1987; Rihm & Henke, 1998), at ~13 Ma (Augustin et al., 2021; Le Pichon & Gaulier, 1988) and ~14 Ma (Delaunay et al., 2023;
Makris & Rihm, 1991). This hypothesis is postulated based on the analysis of magnetic anomalies, gravimetry, bathymetry
and seismic data (Augustin et al., 2016, 2021; Bohannon, 1986; Bohannon & Eittreim, 1991; Delaunay et al., 2023; Izzeldin,
1987; Mitchell & Park, 2014; Mitchell et al., 2023; Okwokwo et al., 2022; Rihm & Henke, 1998).
It represents a very serious hypothesis (the most plausible to me). I don’t know whether there is a feud between you and
these authors, but I think it is not correct to not at least mention it. You don’t have to embrace it (the issue is not settled; these
are still open hypotheses) but at least mention it and acknowledge that this is a possibility or argue why you reject it.
This also has implications for your main message of your paper: the delayed seafloor spreading (see below).
Delayed seafloor spreading
For me, this represents the most important weakness of the manuscript. The delayed seafloor spreading seems to be one of
the most central points of your paper, it is mentioned in the title, in the abstract, and in the last sentences of the paper. But
you did not convince me that seafloor spreading was actually delayed in this part of the Red Sea. You actually never give
arguments to say it was delayed.
Considering that faulting started around 29 Ma (Bohannon, 1986), we have 24 to 15 My between start of rifting and seafloor
spreading (for oceanic spreading starting at 5 and 14 Ma respectively, see above). Is that long? No. Compared to other
margins, this is relatively short (Sapin et al., 2021; Ziegler & Cloetingh, 2004). Was it delayed compared to the rest of the
Red Sea? Not really. The northern Red Sea is thought be several authors to not having reached a steady-state oceanic
spreading yet (e.g. Almalki et al., 2015; Coleman & McGuire, 1988), so the southern Red Sea is not delayed compared to it.
Even more striking, the southernmost Red Sea in the Bab-el-Mandeb/Hanish Island region is delayed compared to your
study area, not having reached oceanic spreading yet and likely not reaching it anytime soon (Rime et al., 2024).
So, if you want to say that seafloor spreading was “significantly delayed”, you’d have to argue for it. But for me, this is not
clear that seafloor spreading was delayed in this area.
Furthermore, I’m not sure magmatic intrusions are the best way to delay oceanic spreading (except for submarine ridges and
oceanic plateau). If you look at a few wide (and long-lived) rifts around the world, you could cite the Basin-and-Range, the
pre-Paleogene Vøring basin (which was the last part of the north Atlantic to break up; Gernigon et al., 2020; Zastrozhnov et
al., 2020), the Santos basin (which was the last part of the south Atlantic to break up; Heine et al., 2013), the South China
Sea (e.g. Chang et al., 2022; Legeay et al., 2024). All these margins were magma-poor (or at least not magma-rich) margins.
The Vøring basin ended up breaking up as magma-rich but the significant pre-Paleogene extension was magma-poor. So,
I’m not sure the mere fact that we observe significant magmatism indicates that the seafloor spreading was delayed.
Instead, I’d say that what you observe here is a very efficient way to accommodate extension with magmatic intrusion
instead of faulting, rather than a way to delay oceanic spreading. So an excellent example of magma-assisted extension or
magmatic rifting, (e.g. Bastow & Keir, 2011; Buck, 2006; Kendall et al., 2005), and a case of magma-compensated-thinning.
And this is still very interesting! Your study shows that these intrusions don’t have much problem ascending through the
crust, they do it fast. That’s interesting because it could imply that if magma is produced, then it is easy for it to accommodate
the extension. And that has important implications for the rifting process because it weakens the crust and allows lower
tectonic forces to complete the breakup (Bialas et al., 2010; Brune et al., 2023; Buck, 2006). The timing is also interesting
because 26 Ma is only 3 Ma younger than the 29 Ma mentioned by Bohannon (1986) for the start of faulting, meaning that
this mechanism can happen quite early in the rifting process. Another very interesting aspect is that your results show the
mechanisms forming a transitional crust (or proto-oceanic as you name it). It might represent the deeper equivalent of some
of what is observed in Greenland for example (Abdelmalak et al., 2015; Brooks, 2011; Hanghøj et al., 2003; Klausen, 2022).
All this to say that even if I am quite sceptical with the delay aspect, I think your results are still very interesting to understand
rifting processes and rift-to-drift transition. So, one way to improve this aspect of the paper would be to step away from this
“delayed” side and concentrate more on the magma-assisted extension side.
SPECIFIC COMMENTS
This rift system began fragmenting the Afro-Arabian shield since the late Oligocene, influenced by a mantle plume impacting
the Afar region around 34 Ma10-12 [Hofmann et al. 1997; Storey 1995; Ebinger & Sleep 1998].
Storey 1995 is definitely not an appropriate reference here as he doesn’t even mention, Ethiopia, Yemen or Afar. (Baker et
al., 1996; Bosworth et al., 2005; Zumbo et al., 1995) would be more appropriate (or just keep the other references you have).
Variations in GNSS-derived relative velocities between the Arabian and Nubian plates, increasing from ~7 mm/yr in the
northern Red Sea to ~16 mm/yr in the southern Red Sea16 [Viltres et al., 2022], may indicate different stages of the rifting
process, suggesting distinct dominant mechanisms for the formation of the northern and southern Red Sea.
Maybe as important is the fact that the northern Red Sea experienced lower total extension. I’d argue that the lower
extension is the cause of the different stages of rifting while the different mechanisms of formation are probably rather
caused by the lower velocity (among other effects such as plume influence). Detail though.
The onset of rifting in the Red Sea was preceded by flood basalts erupted in Ethiopia, NE Sudan and SW Yemen17
[Chauvet et al., 2023],
Chauvet et al., 2023 is maybe not the best reference to cite here as they don’t deal much with the flood basalts or
chronology. Maybe papers such as (Bosworth et al., 2005; Rime et al., 2023; Rooney, 2017) would be more appropriate.
Detail though.
also associated by rhyolitic volcanism until ~26 Ma18,19 [Baker et al., 1996; Manetti et al., 1991].
I’d maybe remove “until ~26 Ma” because rhyolitic volcanism has been recorded until much more recent time in Afar,
including on the Red Sea coast (Lahitte et al., 2003; Varet, 2018). Detail though.
Second comment, I’d maybe add a small sentence around here to indicate the age of faulting along this margin. At the
moment, you only mention the age of magmatic activity, but the reader might also be interested in the age of faulting.
Bohannon (1986) for example mention an age of 23 to 29 Ma for faulting in the area.
along with the contemporaneous Tihama Asir20 [Coleman & McGuire, 1988] (southern Red Sea), Al Lith25 [Pallister, 1987]
(central Red Sea) and Quseir21,22 [Ligi et al., 2018; 2019] (northern Red Sea) magmatic complexes, which include
gabbros, basaltic dikes, and granophyres.
Maybe you could also mention the granite batholiths found in Yemen (Capaldi et al., 1987; Davison et al., 1994) (if the length
of the paper and references allows it)?
Magmatic underplating and crustal contamination
I’m not qualified to discuss the detail of this section, but the aspect of the underplating, cited in the title of the section and
used again in the discussion, is not clearly presented in this section itself. If you mean underplating at the Moho, what proxy
allows you to say there was underplating? If you mean underplating in sense of any ponding within the lower crust (sensu
Thybo & Artemieva, 2013), then what argument do you have for it? You say that there was only little assimilation from the
lower curst (and use it as an argument to say the melts ascended rapidly, see below).
It might be straightforward for an expert, but it is not for me.
Earlier studies proposed that seafloor spreading in the southern Red Sea began with the emplacement of the Tihama Asir
and Al Lith magmatic complexes (26 – 21 Ma), where gabbros and dikes, with a strong geochemical affinity to melts
generated by depleted mantle, could indicate emplacement of oceanic crust beneath much of the Red Sea's coastal plains,
shelf regions and its central axis40,60-62 [Stern & Johnson, 2019; Girdler & Styles, 1974; Almalki et al., 2014; Augustin et
al., 2021].
Not very appropriate to cite Augustin et al. (2021) here as they don’t mention the Tihama Asir and Al Lith complexes at all
and propose the formation of oceanic crust at 13 Ma, i.e. long after their emplacements.
Our results show that syn-rift gabbros formed in relatively shallow magma chambers [...], fuelled by asthenospheric melts that
incorporated ancient lower continental crust material. The minimal contamination from upper crustal material suggests these
melts ascended rapidly through the continental crust with limited interaction.
Also in the Abstract:
the formation of syn-rift gabbros in relatively shallow magma chambers, fed by asthenospheric melts that assimilated ancient
lower continental crustal material. The limited interaction with the upper crust indicates a swift ascent through the continental
crust without significant contamination.
In both cases, you say that these melts incorporated lower continental crustal material and, right after, you say that they had
little interaction with the continental crust. It sounds contradictory to me. If it incorporated lower continental crustal material,
then it did interact with the continental crust. Do you mean it ascended rapidly and had little/no interaction with the upper
crust only? Or you mean that it interacted with the lower crust, but not too much, and thus that it was still rapid (maybe not as
fast as in the upper crust)?
This point of a rapid magma ascend is quite important to your paper. I think that the argumentation should be solid and not
prone to confusion as it is now. You should probably rephrase these parts and/or argue a bit more to explain why you
interpret it ascended rapidly.
I am not an expert, and I might miss something, but the audience of the journal is also very broad and other readers might also
find these statements confusing.
The above indicates a rapid replacement of the continental lithospheric mantle with upwelling asthenosphere,
This point is quite important to your paper, but the argumentation is not clear to me. What argument make you say the
lithospheric mantle was already completely replaced? I miss a step to explain why the melt did not ascend through the
lithospheric mantle before reaching the crust. It seems to me that you never explicitly explain this.
Again, it might be because I’m not an expert, but the reader might also not be one.
Our new findings are crucial because...
A few comments on this paragraph.
I would maybe end the paragraph with a comparison of your results. You mention other examples, but I’d make a more direct
link with your results. “This is comparable with our results …” or “we confirm here these geophysical interpretations with
petrological evidence”. Just a suggestion.
Another paper that you might perhaps want to compare to your work is the recent one of La Rosa et al. (2024), which image
lower crustal intrusion in Afar with a completely different technique (and completely different timescale). Just a suggestion.
BTW, good that you put here a real emphasis on the additional value of your work compared to other publications. This
should also come in the introduction.
Geophysical data, including density, magnetic and seismic velocity anomalies, provide significant constraints...
I would put this paragraph before the one comparing with other examples worldwide. So, you bring all arguments (samples
analyses + geophysics) before comparing with other areas. Now, you have a “lonely” sentence on the topic earlier “This
process is also supported by gravity models explaining Bouguer anomaly patterns64 [Issachar et al., 2023].” and I would say
that the whole paragraph would be better placed replacing this lonely sentence.
Just a suggestion.
In addition, at low extension rates, when migrating melt does not repeatedly intrude the same axial zone, dike intrusions may
increase crustal strength compositionally75,76 [Beutel et al., 2010; Daniels et al., 2014]. This process can accommodate
extension in the upper crust, maintain its thickness, and delay crustal rupturing76 [Daniels et al., 2014].
The “in addition” makes the reader feel these sentences are connected to the previous point. But they are not really. Maybe
better separate these two aspects.
Second comment: as far as I understand these papers, neither Beutel et al., nor Daniels et al. say that migrating intrusions
would increase crustal strength. Daniels et al. only mention that the crust would weaken less if the intrusions are distributed
rather than on repeated at the same place. Overall, most models show that intrusion weaken the crust (Beutel et al., 2010;
Bialas et al., 2010; Brune et al., 2023; Buck, 2006; Daniels et al., 2014)
our work allows to outline the evolution of the southern Red Sea rift and the transition from continental rifting to oceanic
seafloor spreading, driven by interactions between thermal, structural and magmatic processes (Fig. 5)...
The paragraph following this sentence explains the process of rifting and drifting in the southern Red Sea citing multiple
papers, but it would benefit if you would explain a bit more clearly which parts are coming from your analyses. I think you
should “sell” your work a bit better and make super clear for the reader what you bring to the story. At the moment, this
paragraph sounds a bit like a review. I’d add sentences like “we show here that …” within the paragraph to really show what
aspects are new in this paper.
Another aspect of this paragraph is that you seem very (too) confident of your model. I’d tone down several statements which

thinning upper continental lithosphere”, “The combination of thermal softening and ductile flow of the lower crust [possibly]
led to depth-dependent, less localized and more distributed deformation, protracting crustal extension and favoring the
development of a wide rifted margin”, “…within the slowly diverging Nubia-Arabia continental lithosphere [probably]

caused rift axis migration

accommodating plate separation by re-thickening the thinned lower crust and compensating for extension through

such as the eastern branch of the East African Rift84 [Bastow & Kier, 2011],

rupture in the Red Sea" by Alessio Sanfilippo and others, and I thank both the editor and authors for
the opportunity to contemplate on this manuscript and provide some feedback. In this manuscript,
the authors present new argon dates, magnetic data, geochemical data including bulk rock elemental,

Tihama Asir igneous complex in Saudi Arabia within the broader context of Red Sea formation and ocean

authors outline an evolution of the Red Sea spanning the Oligocene-Miocene wherein the variable
spreading rates of the Southern and Northern Red Sea are explained by weakening of the lithosphere
in the south due to impingement of the Afar Plume and collision in the north of the plate. Thermal
weakening of lithosphere combined with asthenospheric upwelling initiated magmatism that

Sanfilippo et al. present a manuscript on a Cenozoic magmatic complex on the passive margin of
the Red Sea. This structure is one of the few rift-related igneous complexes cropping out and available
to study magma-rich rifting processes and the rift-to-drift transition. They apply petrological,
geochemical and isotopic methods to investigate the emplacement of this igneous complex, including
melt pathways and crustal contamination. They derive a model for the formation of the Red Sea passive
margin, where the magmatic intrusions increase the thickness of the crust, forming a proto-oceanic
crust. They finally propose that these magmatic intrusions delay seafloor spreading. Overall, the
object of the study is rare, interesting, and its analysis is novel. The topic will appeal to a broad range
of geologists working on rift and passive margins and won’t be limited to igneous petrologists only.
I am not qualified to judge the methodology. The links between the results and some of the
interpretations are not clear to me. This does not necessarily mean that these interpretations are
wrong, but maybe that this link is not explicitly phrased for non-experts. I’ll leave the other reviewer(s)
judge the validity of these aspects, but I encourage the authors to rephrase these argumentations for
the broader audience.

spreading. I question this interpretation as the delayed nature of oceanic spreading in the southern
Red Sea is far from clear and several arguments indicate a rather quick transition to oceanic
spreading compared to other margins worldwide and other parts of the Red Sea. The link between
magmatism and delay is also not clear. I would advise the authors to either leave out this part of the
interpretation and focus on other interesting aspects, such as magma-assisted extension, or to present
a robust argumentation.

the extent and the age of oceanic spreading in the Red Sea and I think this should be corrected. More
detailed comments are listed below.
