interpretation of rapid continental lithospheric mantle replacement by upwelling asthenosphere.
Additionally, the evidence of limited lower crustal contamination and the absence of upper crustal
assimilation imply short magma residence times within the upper continental crust, consistent with
rapid ascent of melts. These interpretations are explicitly discussed and supported throughout the
Results and Discussion sections of the manuscript.
“Age of oceanic spreading in the Red Sea”
One important paragraph of the paper deals with the age of oceanic spreading in the Red Sea.
You conclude that oceanic spreading started around 5 Ma. The problem is that you omit one of the
main hypotheses about the structure of the (southern) Red Sea. In the paper, you present two
hypotheses, the 5 Ma oceanic crust hypothesis and the “two-stage” oceanic crust hypothesis. I agree
with you that the latter is not plausible from a timing and kinematic point of view (you could even
shorten this argumentation if you’d need more space). But you completely omit the hypothesis of an
onset of oceanic spreading between 10 and 14 Ma. This hypothesis has seen a lot of attention since
the 80s and in the last decade. Many serious publications argue for such an interpretation. They
estimate the initiation of seafloor spreading around 10 Ma (Okwokwo et al., 2022), between 10-12 Ma
(Izzeldin, 1987; Rihm & Henke, 1998), at ~13 Ma (Augustin et al., 2021; Le Pichon & Gaulier, 1988)
and ~14 Ma (Delaunay et al., 2023; Makris & Rihm, 1991). This hypothesis is postulated based on
the analysis of magnetic anomalies, gravimetry, bathymetry and seismic data (Augustin et al., 2016,
2021; Bohannon, 1986; Bohannon & Eittreim, 1991; Delaunay et al., 2023; Izzeldin, 1987; Mitchell
& Park, 2014; Mitchell et al., 2023; Okwokwo et al., 2022; Rihm & Henke, 1998). It represents a very
serious hypothesis (the most plausible to me). I don’t know whether there is a feud between you and
these authors, but I think it is not correct to not at least mention it. You don’t have to embrace it (the
issue is not settled; these are still open hypotheses) but at least mention it and acknowledge that this
is a possibility or argue why you reject it. This also has implications for your main message of your
paper: the delayed seafloor spreading (see below).
We fully agree with the Reviewer that this is an important issue that merits discussion in the
manuscript. Its omission was not intentional but rather a consequence of the strict space limitations
of Nature Geoscience, where the manuscript was initially submitted before being transferred to
Nature Communications. Although we consider the second hypothesis (seafloor spreading initiating
around 5–6 Ma, see Ligi et al., 2019 for further details) to be more consistent with the available
geophysical data, we acknowledge the validity of the alternative interpretation suggesting an earlier
onset (10–14 Ma). We would also like to clarify that the corresponding author has co-authored several
publications on the Red Sea with both Dr. Mitchell and Dr. Augustin, with whom we maintain a
collegial and collaborative relationship. Therefore, there were no other reasons (scientific or personal)
for not including this hypothesis in the discussion. In the revised version, we have now explicitly
addressed this viewpoint and referenced the recent relevant studies to provide a more balanced and
comprehensive treatment of this ongoing debate adding the paragraph below at the beginning of the
Discussion section.
“The evolution of the Red Sea rift has been debated for over 50 years, with no definitive evidence
confirming the nature of the underlying crust14,46 [Ligi et al., 2019; Augustin et al., 2021 and references
herein]. Even in recent publications, significant uncertainty remains regarding the extent of oceanic
crust within the basin. Some researchers support a fully oceanic regime extending
along the entire Red Sea basin since 14–10 Ma46-48 [e.g., Augustin et al., 2021; Okwokwo et al., 2022;
Delaunay et al., 2023], while others propose that attenuated continental crust persisted until 6–5 Ma,
when seafloor spreading initiated in the southern and central Red Sea [e.g., Le Magoarou et al.,
49-51
2021; Ali et al., 2023; Issachar et al., 2023]. Both hypotheses are based on similar datasets including
magnetic, gravity, bathymetric, and seismic data, yet no borehole samples exist to conclusively
determine the nature of the crust beneath the main trough. Furthermore, gravity and magnetic
signatures are ambiguous and can be attributed to either oceanic or continental sources. The thick,
high-velocity evaporite sequence also limits the resolution of multichannel seismic reflection
profiles, obscuring the basement's tectonic architecture and hindering efforts to resolve its origin.”
“Delayed seafloor spreading”
For me, this represents the most important weakness of the manuscript. The delayed seafloor
spreading seems to be one of the most central points of your paper, it is mentioned in the title, in the
abstract, and in the last sentences of the paper. But you did not convince me that seafloor spreading
was actually delayed in this part of the Red Sea. You actually never give arguments to say it was
delayed. Considering that faulting started around 29 Ma (Bohannon, 1986), we have 24 to 15 My
between start of rifting and seafloor spreading (for oceanic spreading starting at 5 and 14 Ma
respectively, see above). Is that long? No. Compared to other margins, this is relatively short (Sapin et al., 2021; Ziegler & Cloetingh, 2004). Was it delayed compared to the rest of the Red Sea? Not
really. The northern Red Sea is thought be several authors to not having reached a steady-state
oceanic spreading yet (e.g. Almalki et al., 2015; Coleman & McGuire, 1988), so the southern Red Sea
is not delayed compared to it. Even more striking, the southernmost Red Sea in the Bab-el-
Mandeb/Hanish Island region is delayed compared to your study area, not having reached oceanic
spreading yet and likely not reaching it anytime soon (Rime et al., 2024). So, if you want to say that
seafloor spreading was “significantly delayed”, you’d have to argue for it. But for me, this is not clear
that seafloor spreading was delayed in this area. Furthermore, I’m not sure magmatic intrusions are
the best way to delay oceanic spreading (except for submarine ridges and oceanic plateau). If you
look at a few wide (and long-lived) rifts around the world, you could cite the Basin-and-Range, the
pre-Paleogene Vøring basin (which was the last part of the north Atlantic to break up; Gernigon et
al., 2020; Zastrozhnov et al., 2020), the Santos basin (which was the last part of the south Atlantic to
break up; Heine et al., 2013), the South China Sea (e.g. Chang et al., 2022; Legeay et al., 2024). All
these margins were magma-poor (or at least not magma-rich) margins. The Vøring basin ended up
breaking up as magma-rich but the significant pre-Paleogene extension was magma-poor. So, I’m not
sure the mere fact that we observe significant magmatism indicates that the seafloor spreading was
delayed.
Instead, I’d say that what you observe here is a very efficient way to accommodate extension
with magmatic intrusion instead of faulting, rather than a way to delay oceanic spreading. So an
excellent example of magma-assisted extension or magmatic rifting, (e.g. Bastow & Keir, 2011; Buck,
2006; Kendall et al., 2005), and a case of magma-compensated-thinning. And this is still very
interesting! Your study shows that these intrusions don’t have much problem ascending through the
crust, they do it fast. That’s interesting because it could imply that if magma is produced, then it is
easy for it to accommodate the extension. And that has important implications for the rifting process
because it weakens the crust and allows lower tectonic forces to complete the breakup (Bialas et al.,
2010; Brune et al., 2023; Buck, 2006). The timing is also interesting because 26 Ma is only 3 Ma
younger than the 29 Ma mentioned by Bohannon (1986) for the start of faulting, meaning that this
mechanism can happen quite early in the rifting process. Another very interesting aspect is that your
results show the mechanisms forming a transitional crust (or proto-oceanic as you name it). It might
represent the deeper equivalent of some of what is observed in Greenland for example (Abdelmalak
et al., 2015; Brooks, 2011; Hanghøj et al., 2003; Klausen, 2022). All this to say that even if I am quite
sceptical with the delay aspect, I think your results are still very
interesting to understand rifting processes and rift-to-drift transition. So, one way to improve this
aspect of the paper would be to step away from this “delayed” side and concentrate more on the
magma-assisted extension side.
We fully agree with the Reviewer’s argument that continental rupture in the southern Red Sea was
indeed delayed (15-20 Ma later the beginning of faulting) when compared to other wide rifted margins
(mostly magma-poor rifted basin), as well as to other segments of the Red Sea itself, such as the
northern Red Sea, which remains in a stage of continental rifting, and the southernmost part near the
Bab-el-Mandeb/Hanish Island region. Our objective was to highlight a significant delay in continental
breakup in the Tihama Asir region, particularly when compared to interpretations that suggest
oceanization began contemporaneously with the emplacement of the magmatic complex.
That said, we have fully incorporated all of the Reviewer's suggestions by refocusing the central
message of the paper on our key observations. The Tihama Asir region provides a clear example of
magma-compensated lithospheric thinning during magma-rich rifting, where extension is efficiently
accommodated through magma underplating, re-thickening the thinning lower continental crust, and
through magmatic intrusions into the extended upper crust, rather than by faulting. To reflect this, we
have changed the title of the paper, rewritten the Abstract, and revised the Discussion to emphasize
these main points. Additionally, we have introduced a new Figure 6 and Supplementary Figure 4.
Figure 6 displays the distribution of magnetic anomalies in the region, together with a geological cross-
section derived from 3D commercial seismic data across the Tihama Asir coastal plain, which
highlights the lack of large faulted extensional blocks within the syn-rift sequence of the Jizan Group.
Supplementary Figure 4 offers a present-day 3D view of the southern Red Sea, visually illustrating
the concept of magma-assisted rifting.
Specific comments
“This rift system began fragmenting the Afro-Arabian shield since the late Oligocene,
influenced by a mantle plume impacting the Afar region around 34 Ma10-12 [Hofmann et al. 1997;
Storey 1995; Ebinger & Sleep 1998]“. Storey 1995 is definitely not an appropriate reference here as
he doesn’t even mention, Ethiopia, Yemen or Afar. (Baker et al., 1996; Bosworth et al., 2005; Zumbo
et al., 1995) would be more appropriate (or just keep the other references you have)
We agree with the Referee’s suggestion to remove the reference to Storey (1995) and to include
Bosworth et al. (2005) instead.
“Variations in GNSS-derived relative velocities between the Arabian and Nubian plates,
increasing from ~7 mm/yr in the northern Red Sea to ~16 mm/yr in the southern Red Sea16 [Viltres
et al., 2022], may indicate different stages of the rifting process, suggesting distinct dominant
mechanisms for the formation of the northern and southern Red Sea“. Maybe as important is the
fact that the northern Red Sea experienced lower total extension. I’d argue that the lower
extension is the cause of the different stages of rifting while the different mechanisms of formation are probably
rather caused by the lower velocity (among other effects such as plume influence). Detail though.
We are not entirely certain we understand this comment, as the amount of extension and plate
separation velocity are closely linked during rifting. Nevertheless, we have revised the sentence in line
with the Reviewer’s suggestion.
“The onset of rifting in the Red Sea was preceded by flood basalts erupted in Ethiopia, NE
Sudan and SW Yemen17 [Chauvet et al., 2023]“. Chauvet et al., 2023 is maybe not the best reference
to cite here as they don’t deal much with the flood basalts or chronology. Maybe papers such as
(Bosworth et al., 2005; Rime et al., 2023; Rooney, 2017) would be more appropriate. Detail though.
We have replaced the reference to Chavet et Al. (2023) with Bosworth et al. (2005).
“also associated by rhyolitic volcanism until ~26 Ma18,19 [Baker et al., 1996; Manetti et al.,
1991].“. I’d maybe remove “until ~26 Ma” because rhyolitic volcanism has been recorded until much
more recent time in Afar, including on the Red Sea coast (Lahitte et al., 2003; Varet, 2018). Detail
though.
We agree that rhyolitic volcanism in the Afar region has continued beyond ~26 Ma, as supported by
the cited studies (e.g., Lahitte et al., 2003; Varet, 2018). In response, we have removed the phrase
“until ~26 Ma”.
Second comment, I’d maybe add a small sentence around here to indicate the age of faulting
along this margin. At the moment, you only mention the age of magmatic activity, but the reader might
also be interested in the age of faulting. Bohannon (1986) for example mention an age of 23 to 29 Ma
for faulting in the area.
We have added a sentence in the Results section that includes the initial age of faulting along this
margin suggested by Bohannon (1986), following the sentence on the emplacement age of the Tihama
Asir volcanic complex.
“along with the contemporaneous Tihama Asir [Coleman & McGuire, 1988] (southern Red
Sea), Al Lith [Pallister, 1987] (central Red Sea) and Quseir [Ligi et al., 2018; 2019] (northern Red
Sea) magmatic complexes, which include gabbros, basaltic dikes, and granophyres”. Maybe you could
also mention the granite batholiths found in Yemen (Capaldi et al., 1987; Davison et al., 1994) (if the
length of the paper and references allows it)?
Due to the limited number of references allowed by Nature Communications, we have chosen not to
include the references to the granite batholiths in Yemen by Capaldi et al. (1987) and Davison et al.
(1994).
“Magmatic underplating and crustal contamination”. I’m not qualified to discuss the detail
of this section, but the aspect of the underplating, cited in the title of the section and used again in
the discussion, is not clearly presented in this section itself. If you mean underplating at the Moho,
what proxy allows you to say there was underplating? If you mean underplating in sense of any
ponding within the lower crust (sensu Thybo & Artemieva, 2013), then what argument do you have
for it? You say that there was only little assimilation from the lower curst (and use it as an argument
to say the melts ascended rapidly, see below). It might be straightforward for an expert, but it is not
for me.
In the Introduction section, we clarified that our use of the term underplating follows the definition of
Thybo & Artemieva (2013), referring to any significant ponding of mafic melts within the lower crust,
not necessarily restricted to the Moho level. In the Results section, we present geochemical and
isotopic compositions of the Tihama Asir gabbros, which show minimal interaction with continental
crust but assimilation of lower crust material. This geochemical evidence supports the idea that the
asthenospheric melts feeding the magmatic complex, were emplaced at lower crustal levels, consistent
with underplating sensu Thybo & Artemieva. We recognize that this interpretation may not be
immediately evident to non-specialists, and we have now revised the relevant paragraph in the
Discussion section to clarify this argument.
“Earlier studies proposed that seafloor spreading in the southern Red Sea began with the
emplacement of the Tihama Asir and Al Lith magmatic complexes (26 – 21 Ma), where gabbros and
dikes, with a strong geochemical affinity to melts generated by depleted mantle, could indicate
emplacement of oceanic crust beneath much of the Red Sea's coastal plains, shelf regions and its
central axis [Stern & Johnson, 2019; Girdler & Styles, 1974; Almalki et al., 2014; Augustin et al.,
2021].” Not very appropriate to cite Augustin et al. (2021) here as they don’t mention the Tihama
Asir and Al Lith complexes at all and propose the formation of oceanic crust at 13 Ma, i.e. long after
their emplacements”. A don’t really agree it demonstrates that it delayed the continental rupture. We
are not even sure that the continental rupture is delayed (see above).
We agree that Augustin et al. (2021) is not directly relevant in this context, as they do not discuss the
Tihama Asir and Al Lith magmatic complexes and propose a later onset of oceanic crust formation.
We have therefore removed the citation to Augustin et al. (2021) from this sentence.
“Our results show that syn-rift gabbros formed in relatively shallow magma chambers [...],
fuelled by asthenospheric melts that incorporated ancient lower continental crust material. The
minimal contamination from upper crustal material suggests these melts ascended rapidly through the
continental crust with limited interaction.” Also in the Abstract:”the formation of syn-rift gabbros in
relatively shallow magma chambers, fed by asthenospheric melts that assimilated ancient lower
continental crustal material. The limited interaction with the upper crust indicates a swift ascent
through the continental crust without significant contamination”. In both cases, you say that these
melts incorporated lower continental crustal material and, right after, you say that they had little
interaction with the continental crust. It sounds contradictory to me. If it incorporated lower
continental crustal material, then it did interact with the continental crust. Do you mean it ascended
rapidly and had little/no interaction with the upper crust only? Or you mean that it interacted with the
lower crust, but not too much, and thus that it was still rapid (maybe not as fast as in the upper crust)?
This point of a rapid magma ascend is quite important to your paper. I think that the argumentation
should be solid and not prone to confusion as it is now. You should probably rephrase these parts
and/or argue a bit more to explain why you interpret it ascended rapidly. I am not an expert, and I
might miss something, but the audience of the journal is also very broad and other readers might also
find these statements confusing.
We disagree with the Referee’s observation, as we do not see a contradiction in our statement. Our
results show that the melts forming the most primitive gabbros and the cross-cutting dykes exhibit
some contamination from the lower crust and no evidence of interaction with the upper crust. In
contrast, the sheeted dikes (overlying the gabbros) display interaction with the upper crust. This overall
pattern of crustal contamination supports our interpretation that the asthenospheric melt ascended and
were emplaced relatively rapidly through the upper continental crust, reducing the time available for
assimilation.
“The above indicates a rapid replacement of the continental lithospheric mantle with upwelling
asthnosphere” This point is quite important to your paper, but the argumentation is not clear to me.
What argument make you say the lithospheric mantle was already completely replaced? I miss a step
to explain why the melt did not ascend through the lithospheric mantle before reaching the crust. It
seems to me that you never explicitly explain this. Again, it might be because I’m not an expert, but
the reader might also not be one.
We thank the Referee for this comment and agree that this point is central to our interpretation. To
address this, we have rewritten the relevant paragraph to explicitly clarify why we infer a complete
replacement of the continental lithospheric mantle by upwelling asthenosphere. The revised text now
reads: “We show here that the rise of asthenosphere enabled the rapid replacement of the continental
lithospheric mantle, as indicated by the geochemical and isotopic compositions of the Tihama Asir
primitive gabbros and dykes cross-cutting the gabbro bodies, which show no evidence of interaction
with continental mantle but only assimilation of lower crust material. The ascent of asthenosphere
resulted in decompression partial melting, producing tholeiitic melts that underplated the lower
continental crust and fed the gabbroic intrusions and basaltic dikes of the Tihama Asir and Al Lith
magmatic complexes, as well as the dike swarms extending along the entire Red Sea coast of Arabia.”
“Our new findings are crucial because....“. A few comments on this paragraph. I would maybe
end the paragraph with a comparison of your results. You mention other examples, but I’d make a
more direct link with your results. “This is comparable with our results ...” or “we confirm here these
geophysical interpretations with petrological evidence”. Just a suggestion.
Another paper that you might perhaps want to compare to your work is the recent one of La
Rosa et al. (2024), which image lower crustal intrusion in Afar with a completely different technique
(and completely different timescale). Just a suggestion. BTW, good that you put here a real emphasis
on the additional value of your work compared to other publications. This should also come in the
introduction.
We revised the text according to the referee’s suggestions by adding a sentence at the end of the
paragraph summarizing the main findings of La Rosa et al. (2025), and by placing more emphasis on
comparing our work with previous publications.
“Geophysical data, including density, magnetic and seismic velocity anomalies, provide
significant constraints... “. I would put this paragraph before the one comparing with other examples
worldwide. So, you bring all arguments (samples analyses + geophysics) before comparing with
other areas. Now, you have a “lonely” sentence on the topic earlier “This process is also supported
by gravity models explaining Bouguer anomaly patterns64 [Issachar et al., 2023].” and I would say
that the whole paragraph would be better placed replacing this lonely sentence. Just a suggestion.
In agreement with the Referee’s suggestion, we have reorganized the manuscript by relocating the
entire section on geophysical data analysis and interpretation before the discussion comparing our
results with global examples.
“In addition, at low extension rates, when migrating melt does not repeatedly intrude the same
axial zone, dike intrusions may increase crustal strength compositionally [Beutel et al., 2010; Daniels
et al., 2014]. This process can accommodate extension in the upper crust, maintain its thickness,
and delay crustal rupturing [Daniels et al., 2014]”. The “in addition” makes the reader feel these
sentences are connected to the previous point. But they are not really. Maybe better separate these
two aspects. Second comment: as far as I understand these papers, neither Beutel et al., nor Daniels
et al. say that migrating intrusions would increase crustal strength. Daniels et al. only mention that
the crust would weaken less if the intrusions are distributed rather than on repeated at the same place.
Overall, most models show that intrusion weaken the crust (Beutel et al., 2010; Bialas et al., 2010;
Brune et al., 2023; Buck, 2006; Daniels et al., 2014).
We have moved this sentence to the following paragraph to improve clarity, and we have rephrased
it and corrected the citations in accordance with the Referee’s comments.
“our work allows to outline the evolution of the southern Red Sea rift and the transition from
continental rifting to oceanic seafloor spreading, driven by interactions between thermal, structural
and magmatic processes (Fig. 5)...”. The paragraph following this sentence explains the process of
rifting and drifting in the southern Red Sea citing multiple papers, but it would benefit if you would
explain a bit more clearly which parts are coming from your analyses. I think you should “sell” your
work a bit better and make super clear for the reader what you bring to the story. At the moment, this
paragraph sounds a bit like a review. I’d add sentences like “we show here that ...” within the
paragraph to really show what aspects are new in this paper.
We have revised the paragraph as suggested by Referee.
Another aspect of this paragraph is that you seem very (too) confident of your model. I’d tone
down several statements which are not proved but suggested. E.g. “Plume-related thermal anomalies
and underplating [probably] initially weakened the lower crust, allowing decoupling between the
lower crust and the lithospheric mantle along the axial zone beneath the thinning upper
continental lithosphere”, “The combination of thermal softening and ductile flow of the lower crust
[possibly] led to depth-dependent, less localized and more distributed deformation, protracting crustal
extension and favoring the development of a wide rifted margin”, “...within the slowly diverging
Nubia-Arabia continental lithosphere [probably] contributed significantly to rift initiation,
accommodating plate separation by re-thickening...”, “...magmatic additions [probably] further
widened the Red Sea basin and [possibly] caused rift axis migration...” These comments also apply to
the caption of Fig. 5.
We agree that some statements in the paragraph, as well as in the caption of former Fig. 5 (Fig. 7 in
the revised manuscript), were overly assertive considering the interpretative nature of the model. In
response, we have revised the text to adopt a more cautious and balanced tone to reflect the
hypothetical nature of the proposed processes and to clearly distinguish interpretation from
observation. The caption of new Fig. 7 has also been adjusted accordingly.
“caused rift axis migration”. Do we really have evidence of rift migration? Or do you infer this
from modelling paper you cite? I’d see another possibility where, instead of rift migration, we have
rift focusing.
Ok, rift focusing.
“accommodating plate separation by re-thickening the thinned lower crust and compensating
for extension through widespread dike intrusions in the upper crust.”. This phrasing implies that the
crust thinned and then became thicker after the intrusions (in two phases). But everything might
happen at the same time and the thinning is only reduced by the intrusions. Maybe the notion of
“magma-compensated thinning” would be more appropriate?
We have chosen to retain the original phrasing, as we believe it does not imply a specific temporal
sequence. The processes described encompass two interconnected phases: an initial stage of
lithospheric thinning and asthenospheric upwelling, followed by magmatic underplating and intrusion.
These magmatic additions may have occurred contemporaneously with crustal thinning and acted to
compensate for it.
“Seafloor spreading commenced approximately 5 Ma in the axial trough of the southern Red
Sea”. As mentioned in the general comments, that’s only one hypothesis. There are others.
We have revised the text to include both current hypotheses for the timing of seafloor spreading
initiation: 6-5 Ma or 10-14 Ma.
“such as the eastern branch of the East African Rift [Bastow & Kier, 2011]”. I’d say “Afar
Depression” rather than “eastern branch of the EAR” as most of the Afar is not part of the EAR sensu
stricto. Detail though.
Ok, Afar Depression.
“Magmatic intrusions in the lower crust delay the localization of lithospheric extension and the
final drifting stage by several million years”. You have not convinced me that these intrusions delay
strain localization. As said above, it is far from certain that oceanic spreading started at 5 Ma in the
Red Sea. If the age of onset of seafloor spreading is 14 Ma, then there is only 7-12 Ma between the
intrusions and seafloor spreading. See general comment at the start of the review.
Please, see our response to this point in the Referee’s General Comment section.
“(Abstract) Our study demonstrates that magmatic underplating during the early rifting phases
significantly delayed the continental rupture and the onset of seafloor spreading in the southern Red
Sea.”. A don’t really agree it demonstrates that it delayed the continental rupture. We are not even
sure that the continental rupture is delayed (see above).
The Abstract has been completely rewritten to take into account the Referee’s suggestions. For details,
please see our response in the Referee’s General Comments section.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Magmatism’s role in continental rupture and ocean formation remains a critical question in Earth Sciences. The Red Sea, where Arabia is rifting from Nubia, offers an ideal setting to explore this process. This study analyses geochemical and isotopic data from gabbros and basaltic dikes in the Tihama Asir complex, formed during early Red Sea rifting (Late Oligocene). The results show that asthenospheric melts assimilated ancient lower crust before rising into shallow magma chambers with minimal upper crustal contamination. Rising asthenosphere driven by the Afar plume and by extensional stresses thermally weakened the lower crust, allowing it to decouple from the mantle, causing depth-dependent deformation. The generated asthenospheric melts underplated and intruded the thinning continental crust protracting continental rifting by re-thickening of the crust and accommodating extension. This study provides the evidence of tholeiitic underplating beneath thick continental crust during early rifting, substantially postponing the onset of seafloor spreading.

---

## Introduction

Over billions of years, the Earth’s internal processes cyclically formed and broke apart supercontinents, leading to the birth of new oceans. The Wilson Cycle explains how continents split, forming passive margins1,2. Continental fragmentation takes place due to extensional stress, initiating rifts where the lithosphere is affected by progressive mechanical deformation and magmatic processes. This process continues until the continental lithosphere ultimately fractures, creating new oceanic lithosphere that separates two conjugate juvenile continental margins. The East African Rift System, including the Red Sea, represents various stages of this process, from continental rifts to an emerging ocean. This rift system began fragmenting the Afro-Arabian shield since the late Oligocene, influenced by a mantle plume impacting the Afar region around 34 Ma3–5. Magnetic anomalies in the Red Sea suggest an ongoing formation of oceanic crust, with the southern region reaching further in this process than the central or northern regions6–8. Variations in the amount of extension may reflect different stages of the rifting process, while differences in GNSS-derived relative velocities between the Arabian and Nubian plates, increasing from ~7 mm/yr in the northern Red Sea to ~16 mm/yr in the southern Red Sea9 suggest distinct dominant mechanisms for the formation of the northern and southern Red Sea. The onset of rifting in the Red Sea was preceded by flood basalts erupted in Ethiopia, NE Sudan, and SW Yemen5, also associated with rhyolitic volcanism10,11. Abundant melt was injected into the Arabian basement in the early stages of rifting (26–21 Ma)5,12–15 as testified by the occurrence of thousands of kilometers-long dike swarms running NW-SE parallel to the Arabian coast of the Red Sea12,16, along with the contemporaneous Tihama Asir12 (southern Red Sea), Al Lith16 (central Red Sea), and Quseir13,14 (northern Red Sea) magmatic complexes, which include gabbros, basaltic dikes, and granophyres. Widespread gabbro and dike injection was followed by successive phases of volcanism, leading to the formation of extensive alkali-basalt lava fields (harrats). Some of these phases had finite eruption periods, while others began at different times and continued into recent history12,16–20 (Fig. 1).

The formation of a magma-rich margin during rifting is driven by multiple geological factors21,22. A key factor is the magmatic supply, where sufficient magma generation from the mantle is essential for processes like dike injection and underplating (i.e., addition of mafic magma to the lower crust and uppermost mantle around the Moho in the form of batholiths and sill-like structures23). Efficient heat transfer from the mantle can promote localized melting and assimilation of crustal material, affecting the formation of transitional crust. The composition and thickness of the pre-existing continental crust affect how it interacts with ascending magmas, while the rheological properties of the lithosphere, such as its strength and viscosity, impact deformation behavior. The duration of rifting, the divergence rate and magmatic activity also play a critical role24. Understanding these constraints is fundamental for modeling magma-rich margin formation and predicting their evolution.

The Tihama Asir magmatic complex in southernmost Saudi Arabia serves as a key location to study the initial phase of syn-rift magmatism and its influence on the geodynamic evolution of the southern Red Sea rift system (Fig. 1), and, more broadly, of magma-rich rift systems. This region provides insights into the interplay between magmatic supply, tectonic setting, heat transfer, and crustal composition during the early stages of rifting12. In this study, we present geochemical data including bulk rock major and trace elements, as well as Sr, Nd, and Pb isotopic compositions of the Tihama Asir gabbros and dykes, in order to investigate the magma source and its migration and emplacement within the crust during rifting. We also measured the magnetic properties of these rocks to better constrain the geophysical signals they produce. Additionally, 40Ar/39Ar age determinations, combined with existing geophysical data, enable us to reconstruct the evolution of the magmatic complex within the broader framework of Red Sea rifting and ocean basin development.

---

## Results

The Tihama Asir igneous complex
The Tihama Asir magmatic complex is located east of the Jizan coastal plain in southwestern Saudi Arabia (Fig. 1). It consists of various layered gabbroic bodies with compositional layering ranging from relatively primitive olivine gabbros to more evolved lithologies such as oxide gabbros, with layering occurring at meter- to decameter-scale and tending to diminish up-section, akin to typical Penrose-type ophiolite stratigraphy25–27. The gabbros are in primary contact with granophyre granitic intrusions, with preserved intrusive contacts to the strongly faulted Arabian Shield Neoproterozoic basement comprising Pan-African granitoids, low-grade metamorphic rocks, and gneisses26. Diffuse basaltic to rhyolitic dike swarms locally overlay the gabbroic lithologies and intrude the continental basement12,26,27. Our 40Ar/39Ar age determination of 26.03±0.54 Ma and recalibrated previous 40Ar/39Ar datings28 of the Tihama Asir intrusive rocks and the dike swarms constrain their age to within the range 26–21 Ma (Supplementary Fig. S1; Supplementary Data S1). Faulting in this area is suggested to have begun around 29 Ma15, just a few million years prior to the formation of the magmatic complex. This temporal relationship implies that the Tihama Asir magmatic complex formed due to extensive magmatism during the early stages of Red Sea continental rifting12,27–29.

Petrology and geochemistry
The most primitive Tihama Asir olivine gabbros show petrological and geochemical characteristics consistent with formation from tholeiitic parental melts, resembling modern MORBs (Supplementary Data S2). However, the evolved gabbros and oxide gabbros show saturation of phlogopite and selective enrichments in LREE and highly incompatible elements (Rb, Ba, U, Th, Nb, Sr, K). The geochemical evolution of the parental melts diverged progressively from that of oceanic tholeiites, suggesting a gradual assimilation of continental crust during the emplacement of the gabbroic bodies (Fig. 2). Similarly, the dike swarms overlying the gabbros (sheeted dike complex) exhibit transitional affinity, with selective enrichments in LREE and highly incompatible elements compared to Red Sea MORB and sub-chondritic Nb-Ta/LREE ratios. These dikes are in chemical equilibrium with the clinopyroxene in the gabbros and are interpreted as melts extracted from hybridized gabbroic crystal mush after high degrees of contamination from upper crustal material.

Furthermore, meter-scale anastomosed basaltic dikes crosscut the gabbros with irregular chilled boundaries, locally dissecting and embaying portions of the host rock (e.g., TA-02/Dy-1; see Fig. 2c). These basalts display a chemical composition indicative of limited fractionation in magma chambers and nearly flat PM-normalized incompatible trace element patterns, akin to present-day enriched MORBs31 (Fig. 2). Being close to chemical equilibrium with the clinopyroxene from the most primitive gabbros, these basalts are considered poorly fractionated mantle melts that escaped crustal contamination and were injected into the cooling gabbroic crystal mush soon after its emplacement30.

Radiogenic isotopes
The Tihama Asir gabbros exhibit higher initial (i.e., present-day values recalculated to their crystallization age; Supplementary Data S3) 87Sr/86Sr (0.7033–0.7037) and lower initial 143Nd/144Nd (0.51292–0.51296) ratios compared to those of Red Sea MORB32–34 and the Cenozoic alkaline magmatism in the northern Arabian plate19,20,35–40. Nonetheless, their initial 206Pb/204Pb and 207Pb/204Pb ratios plot amongst the most depleted samples from the Red Sea MORB and the Cenozoic volcanism from northern Arabia (Fig. 3). The gabbros isotopically resemble the inferred compositions of the Afar plume41–43 in terms of Nd and Sr isotopes, albeit they are less radiogenic in Pb. These compositions (Supplementary Data S3) suggest a source with relatively high time-integrated Rb/Sr and low Sm/Nd ratios compared to those of the northern Red Sea basalts, but with similarly low U–Th/Pb ratios. Interestingly, a basaltic dike (TA-02/Dy-1) cutting across the gabbros exhibits Sr–Nd–Pb isotopes nearly coincident with those of the inferred Afar plume (Fig. 3), supporting the idea that primary melts of the Tihama Asir formed from an asthenospheric source near the main impingement area of the Afar plume30. Upon closer examination, selected gabbroic samples gradually diverge from the crosscutting dike along trends of decreasing Sr–Nd and Pb isotope ratios. These isotopic signatures suggest contamination by material with ancient depletions in Rb/Sr and U/Th/Pb, coupled with relatively low Sm/Nd ratios, compositions commonly attributed to lower continental crustal material, such as the ancient lower continental crustal granulite xenoliths locally sampled within the Cenozoic volcanism of the Arabian plate25.

In contrast, samples from the sheeted dike complex have much higher initial 87Sr/86Sr (0.7038–0.7047) and lower initial 143Nd/144Nd (0.51284–0.51293) ratios compared to those of gabbros, yet they exhibit similar Pb isotope ratios. These samples cluster within the Nd–Sr and Pb isotopic space of the widespread volcanism in South Arabia and Yemen, well-known examples of Afar-type magma strongly contaminated by both upper and lower continental crust41,42. Given that these rocks display intrusive contacts with upper crustal lithologies and show selective enrichments in highly incompatible elements and LREE compared to the gabbros, we infer that their melts were generated within melt-rich zones of the gabbroic crystal mush and might have further assimilated Pan-African upper continental crust. Indeed, their Sr–Nd-Pb compositions fall between those of the Tihama Asir intrusives and the Pan-African granitoids (Fig. 3). Our hypothesis is corroborated by combined radiogenic Nd–Sr–Pb and δ18O isotopes of flood volcanics from Yemen42, which exhibit the same extent of isotopic variations observed in the Tihama Asir gabbros (Fig. 3). The less contaminated Yemenite basalts retain mantle-like δ18O isotopes and Sr–Nd and Pb isotopic ratios indicative of an Afar-like upper mantle. In contrast, those retaining evidence of crustal contamination have high δ18O isotopes42 and diverge along two different trends, aligned towards enriched and depleted Pb compositions, indicating contamination by upper and lower Pan-African crust, respectively.

Assimilation-fractional crystallization model
We conducted assimilation-fractional crystallization (AFC) modeling following the approach outlined by ref. 44. Specifically tailored to simulate the chemical evolution of a magmatic system undergoing fractional crystallization alongside assimilation of wall rocks (Figs. 4 and 5). We utilized the average compositions of lower crustal granulite xenoliths42 and Pan-African granitoids45 as the assimilated components, and the crosscutting basaltic dike displaying Afar-like compositions as the initial melt (for further details, see Methods). The isotopic trends observed in the Tihama Asir gabbros are faithfully reproduced across all different Nd–Sr–Pb isotopic spaces at low degrees of assimilation of lower crustal granulites, considering mass assimilated/mass crystallized ratios ranging from 0.7 to 0.9 (Fig. 4), and utilizing the same geochemical parameters used to replicate the trace element enrichments30.

Conversely, the high Sr and low Nd isotopes observed in the sheeted dikes necessitate additional assimilation of Pan-African granitoids, commencing from the hybrid melts that formed the gabbros. Notably, our model adeptly reproduces the distinct trends of the gabbros and dike swarms concerning Nd and Sr versus ΔPb (7/4) (Fig. 4b). The low 206Pb/204Pb ratios and comparatively high 207Pb/204Pb ratios of lower crustal granulites in the Arabian plate42 result in a gradual increase in ΔPb (7/4) as 143Nd/144Nd ratios decrease. Conversely, the upper crustal Pan-African granitoids have 206Pb/204Pb and 207Pb/204Pb lying on the NHRL45, thus producing a local decrease in ΔPb (7/4).

---

## Methods

40Ar/39Ar dating
Age determinations were performed at the Laboratoire des Sciences du Climat et de l’Environnement facility (CNRS-CEA, Gif-sur-Yvette), France.

Sample preparation
40Ar/39Ar measurements were performed on the microcrystalline groundmass of the sample, considered representative of the phase that crystallized during lava solidification. Samples were crushed, sieved (250–125 mm size), and washed in 1N acetic acid at 60 °C for 40 minutes to remove secondary mineral phases. Phenocrysts and xenocrysts, carrying an excess of 40Ar, were removed using heavy liquids (Diiodomethane) and magnetic separations. Absence of alteration phases was verified using a binocular microscope.

Procedure
Splits of 120–130 mg were wrapped in 99.5% copper foil, loaded in aluminum disks, and irradiated in the CLICIT facility at Oregon State University’s TRIGA reactor for 10 h. After irradiation, samples were degassed at 550-650 °C to remove atmospheric argon. Neutron fluence (J) was monitored using FCs crystals, with J values calculated from 6 single crystal laser fusion analyses, reported in Supplementary Data S1. Age calculations used the decay constants from ref. 75 and an atmospheric 40Ar/36Ar ratio of 298.56 from ref. 76. Precision of mass discrimination correction was monitored by daily air argon measurements, achieving about 0.1–0.15% (1σ standard deviation).

Pure groundmass aliquots were incrementally heated in 10 steps between 650 °C and 1200 °C using a metal resistance furnace. Isotopic measurements were performed using a high-sensitivity GV5400 instrument in ion counting mode. An analytical run consisted of 20 peak scans of each argon isotope with integration times 2 s (40Ar, 39Ar), 10 s (37Ar, 38Ar, baseline) and 20 s (36Ar). This was preceded by a peak centering routine on the five Ar isotopes upon sample admission into the mass spectrometer. Raw argon isotope abundances were regressed back to inlet time using NG software (v. 2.90). System blanks measured prior to step-heating ranged from 6.8×10−16 to 1.2×10−15 moles of 40Ar and 2.5·10-18 to 6.2×10−18 moles of 36Ar, which were substantially lower than sample signals.

Results
Plateau ages, isochron regressions, probability of fit estimates and errors were calculated using ArArCalc77 following the criteria defined in ref. 78. Results of the step heating experiment are detailed in the Supplementary Data S1. The plateau age for sample TA-06/Dy-1, calculated from 66.4% of gas released, excluded the first three and last steps due to anomalously young apparent ages likely caused by 40Ar* loss from subtle alteration. The preferred age for this sample is the plateau age of 26.03±0.54 Ma (2σ uncertainty).

Re-evaluation of Ar–Ar literature dates using updated standards
40Ar/39Ar ages from ref. 28. were originally calibrated against an age of 17.25±0.20 Ma for the Bern 4B biotite standard, which corresponds to an age of 126.6±4.2 Ma for LP-679. Initially, Bern 4B’s age was recalibrated using the ArAR software80, considering an updated age of 127.5 Ma for LP-6, which equates to an age of 28.10±0.04 Ma for FCTs. This recalibration increased the age of Bern 4B to 17.38±0.20 Ma. This age was further recalculated using the FCTs age applied in this study (28.201±0.023 Ma81). Based on this calculation, the age of Bern 4B is adjusted to 17.44±0.20 Ma. This updated age was used to recalculate the ages reported by ref. 28. using the ArAR software. For consistency, we also applied the constant values from ref. 75. in the calculation (Supplementary Data S1).

Bulk rock major, trace elements, and Sr, Nd, and Pb isotope compositions
The bulk rock major and trace element compositions of the Tihama Asir gabbros and sheeted dikes are sourced from ref. 30. and were analyzed using XRF and ICP-mass spectrometry at Activation Laboratories Ltd., Ancaster, Ontario (Supplementary Data S2), following the analytical techniques detailed on the company’s website (www.actlabs.com).

Bulk rock Sr, Nd, and Pb isotope analyses were conducted at the Dipartimento di Scienze della Terra, University of Florence. Sample powders (approximately 250 mg each) were taken from the same aliquots used for major and trace element determinations. The samples were leached with 1M HCl in an ultrasonic bath and rinsed several times with MilliQ water to minimize potential contributions from secondary phases that could have altered the magma signature. The samples were dissolved through sequential HF–HNO3–HCl dissolution, and the Sr, Nd, and Pb fractions were purified through standard liquid chromatographic techniques.

Isotopic ratios were determined using thermal ionization mass spectrometry (Thermo-Fisher Scientific Triton Plus). Mass fractionation of Sr and Nd isotopes was exponentially corrected with 86Sr/88Sr=0.1194 and 146Nd/144Nd=0.7219, respectively. Interferences of 87Rb and 144Sm on 87Sr and 144Nd, respectively, were monitored by measuring 85Rb and 147Sm. Due to their extremely low abundances (when present) these masses were measured on 1013 Ohm amplifiers; such interferences resulted negligible for all the samples. All other masses were measured on 1011 Ohm amplifiers. The within-run 87Sr/86Sr average value for NBS 987 reference material was 0.710255±7 (2σ, n=4), and the 143Nd/144Nd average value for the internal standard NdFi was 0.511465±3 (2σ, n=3). Accuracy and precision were further checked by measuring the isotope ratios of international rock standards BHVO-1 (87Sr/86Sr=0.703484±6; 143Nd/144Nd=0.512986±9) and BCR-2 (87Sr/86Sr=0.705018±7; 143Nd/144Nd=0.512620±5).

Lead isotopic composition was measured by collecting the smaller 204Pb beam on 1013 Ohm amplifier and the other masses (206Pb, 207Pb, and 208Pb) on 1011 Ohm amplifiers. Instrumental mass bias was corrected using replicate analyses of NIST SRM 981 standard, yielding an average fractionation factor of 0.135% (±0.010%) per mass unit relative to the reference values, which was applied to all Pb isotopic ratios. The accuracy of the Pb isotope measurements was tested through replicate analyses of international reference material BHVO-1 (206Pb/204Pb=18.705±4, 207Pb/204Pb=15.577±5, 208Pb/204Pb=38.375±15). All the isotope ratios of the reference materials are reported in Supplementary Data S3 and are identical within error to previously published values82,83.

All the isotope ratios were recalculated to their initial values, assumed to correspond to the time of the rock formation. The formation ages of the studied samples were estimated based on the available Ar–Ar ages of the associated lithological units (this work and recalibrated ages of ref. 28. (Supplementary Data S1). For the age correction, we specifically re-measured the elemental Rb/Sr, Sm/Nd, U/Pb, and Th/Pb ratios on the leached samples using ICP-MS (7800 Agilent) at the University of Florence. A small aliquot of the same sample solution used for isotopic measurements was collected (after complete dissolution and before chemical separation), evaporated, and diluted in 2% HNO3 for ICP-MS analyses. Replicate analyses of international reference materials BHVO-1 and AGV-1 yielded Rb/Sr, U/Pb, Th/Pb, and Sm/Nd ratios consistent with reference values of ref. 84. and with reproducibility <4% (2σ). The internal errors (2σ) of the age-corrected Sr, Nd, and Pb isotope ratios for all samples were fully propagated to account for uncertainties in age, isotopic ratios, and elemental contents. Total procedure blanks for Sr, Nd, and Pb were 60 pg, 12 pg, and 43 pg, respectively. The data and associated uncertainties are reported in Supplementary Data S3.

Assimilation-fractional crystallization model
The enrichments in highly incompatible elements (e.g., Rb, Ba, Th, U, Zr, Hf) and the positive LREE/HREE fractionation observed in the melts in equilibrium with the Tihama Asir clinopyroxenes can be effectively reproduced by a process involving the assimilation of lower and upper continental crust, combined with fractional crystallization of a gabbroic assemblage (i.e., olivine, plagioclase, and clinopyroxene)30. A similar geochemical model is applied here to assess whether the assimilation of lower and upper continental crust can explain the isotopic compositions of the Tihama Asir gabbros and the associated sheeted dike.

The trace element (Sm, Nd, Rb, Sr, Th, U, and Pb) and initial Nd–Sr–Pb isotopic compositions of the melts generated during the two scenarios above (assimilation of lower and/or upper crust) were calculated using an assimilation-fractional crystallization (AFC) process, following the equations of ref. 44. For the assimilation of the lower crust, we used the basalts (TA-02/Dy-1) crosscutting the Tihama Asir gabbros at a high angle as the starting melt composition. These basalts, unmodified by any crustal contamination process, exhibit an EMORB-like trace element pattern and isotopic composition similar to that of the inferred Afar plume43. Conversely, the starting melt composition for the assimilation of upper crust has a Nd–Sr–Pb isotopic composition coinciding with the average isotopic composition of the Tihama Asir gabbros and is similar to melts extracted from the gabbros after 5–10% degrees of lower crustal contamination. The composition of the melt modified by the AFC process was calculated at 1% increments, representing the remaining melt mass (scaled from 100% to 0), corresponding to ‘F’ in the equation from ref. 44. Each of the two AFC scenarios was calculated using the mean and extreme (±1σ) compositions of the lower and upper crust assimilants42,45. The AFC scenarios were modeled with different Ma/Mc ratios of 0.9, 0.8, and 0.7, shown in Fig. 4 in red, blue, and gray, respectively. Parameters and results are provided in Supplementary Data S4.

Magnetic properties
Magnetic properties, including natural remanent magnetization (NRM) and volume-specific magnetic susceptibility (K), were measured on 14 rock samples at the paleomagnetic lab of ISMAR-CNR in Bologna, Italy. Four samples (marked AR) of basaltic dikes were hand-oriented in the field using a magnetic compass. In the laboratory, between 1 and 5 standard paleomagnetic cylinders (2.54×2.2 cm) were drilled from each rock sample, resulting in a total of 31 specimens. The NRM was measured with a PSM spinner magnetometer, while magnetic susceptibility (K) was determined using a Bartington MS2B meter. The Koenigsberger ratio (Q) was calculated as the ratio of remanent magnetization (NRM) to the induced magnetization produced by Earth’s field (26.506 A/m). Results are presented in Supplementary Fig. S3 and Supplementary Data S5.

Data availability
All the data generated in this study are provided in the Supplementary Data files (from S1 to S5) and have also been deposited in Figshare https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.29410169.

Code availability
The Assimilation-fractional crystallization (AFC) model code (alpha-MELTS), which can be used to re-produce the data presented here (Supplementary Data S4), is available on GitHub https://github.com/magmasource/alphaMELTS.

So, if you want to say that seafloor spreading was “significantly delayed”, you’d have to argue for it. But for me, this is not
clear that seafloor spreading was delayed in this area.
Furthermore, I’m not sure magmatic intrusions are the best way to delay oceanic spreading (except for submarine ridges and
oceanic plateau). If you look at a few wide (and long-lived) rifts around the world, you could cite the Basin-and-Range, the
pre-Paleogene Vøring basin (which was the last part of the north Atlantic to break up; Gernigon et al., 2020; Zastrozhnov et
al., 2020), the Santos basin (which was the last part of the south Atlantic to break up; Heine et al., 2013), the South China
Sea (e.g. Chang et al., 2022; Legeay et al., 2024). All these margins were magma-poor (or at least not magma-rich) margins.
The Vøring basin ended up breaking up as magma-rich but the significant pre-Paleogene extension was magma-poor. So,
I’m not sure the mere fact that we observe significant magmatism indicates that the seafloor spreading was delayed.
Instead, I’d say that what you observe here is a very efficient way to accommodate extension with magmatic intrusion
instead of faulting, rather than a way to delay oceanic spreading. So an excellent example of magma-assisted extension or
magmatic rifting, (e.g. Bastow & Keir, 2011; Buck, 2006; Kendall et al., 2005), and a case of magma-compensated-thinning.
And this is still very interesting! Your study shows that these intrusions don’t have much problem ascending through the
crust, they do it fast. That’s interesting because it could imply that if magma is produced, then it is easy for it to accommodate
the extension. And that has important implications for the rifting process because it weakens the crust and allows lower
tectonic forces to complete the breakup (Bialas et al., 2010; Brune et al., 2023; Buck, 2006). The timing is also interesting
because 26 Ma is only 3 Ma younger than the 29 Ma mentioned by Bohannon (1986) for the start of faulting, meaning that
this mechanism can happen quite early in the rifting process. Another very interesting aspect is that your results show the
mechanisms forming a transitional crust (or proto-oceanic as you name it). It might represent the deeper equivalent of some
of what is observed in Greenland for example (Abdelmalak et al., 2015; Brooks, 2011; Hanghøj et al., 2003; Klausen, 2022).
All this to say that even if I am quite sceptical with the delay aspect, I think your results are still very interesting to understand
rifting processes and rift-to-drift transition. So, one way to improve this aspect of the paper would be to step away from this
“delayed” side and concentrate more on the magma-assisted extension side.
